questions.stem: A GenAI firm goes from lab demo to priced API with SLAs and support. In the Four I’s, the priced launch is:

options.A: Innovation because commercialization creates adoption and value capture
options.B: Idea because the concept matters more than a working product
options.C: Imitation because releasing models necessarily copies prior research
options.D: Invention because the artifact exists but markets are not relevant

questions.explanation: Innovation is commercialization of an invention—market launch with adoption/capture.

questions.stem: A company publishes research but never ships products. Under the Four I’s, it is strongest at:

options.A: Invention because journals issue patents
options.B: Imitation because papers force adoption
options.C: Innovation because publications are market launches
options.D: Ideas rather than innovation via commercialization

questions.explanation: Publication fits idea/basic research; innovation requires commercialization and adoption.

questions.stem: A demo-ready prototype fails to convert into repeat sales. Best diagnosis is:

options.A: Imitation without invention (no novelty possible)
options.B: Imitation without ideas (adoption precedes discovery)
options.C: Invention without innovation (commercialization/adoption missing)
options.D: Innovation without invention (markets create artifacts)

questions.explanation: Market adoption and commercialization are required for invention to become innovation.

questions.stem: A fast follower launches after a rival’s success with minor tweaks. In the Four I’s, this is mainly:

options.A: Idea because it is conceptual repositioning
options.B: Imitation of a proven commercialization template
options.C: Innovation because followers are always “new to world”
options.D: Invention because entry transforms copies into novelty

questions.explanation: Fast following typically copies the successful pattern; that is imitation.

questions.stem: A firm expects imitation after success. The best sustaining response is:

options.A: Outsource learning to raise inimitability
options.B: Build complements and continuously innovate beyond the visible feature
options.C: Switch to pipeline because platforms are always copied
options.D: Publish details because disclosure slows competitors

questions.explanation: Sustaining advantage often requires complements and ongoing innovation cycles.

questions.stem: A firm increases R&D but reduces market experimentation. Under speed-of-innovation logic, this likely:

options.A: Speeds learning because labs replace customers
options.B: Eliminates imitation because customers see less
options.C: Guarantees radical innovation by spending more
options.D: Slows learning because feedback cycles lengthen

questions.explanation: Market learning slows when feedback loops weaken, reducing innovation speed.

questions.stem: A firm invents first, but a rival wins by scaling distribution and service. This most directly shows:

options.A: Basic research alone ensures adoption at scale
options.B: Commercialization and diffusion often beat first invention
options.C: Invention is irrelevant once patents exist
options.D: First invention always guarantees capture and dominance

questions.explanation: Diffusion and commercialization capabilities determine who captures value.

questions.stem: A firm patents a recommendation model. The Chapter 7–consistent risk is:

options.A: Disclosure helps rivals learn, eroding advantage
options.B: Disclosure prevents rivals learning, preserving secrecy
options.C: Patents force adoption by lowering buyer risk
options.D: Patents remove substitutes from the category

questions.explanation: Algorithms are often kept secret because patent disclosure can nullify advantage.

questions.stem: A firm ships weekly updates and runs tight A/B tests. The strongest Chapter 7 explanation is:

options.A: Weekly shipping lowers buyer power without affecting learning
options.B: Short feedback loops accelerate learning and innovation speed
options.C: Weekly shipping eliminates substitutes by changing too fast
options.D: Weekly shipping blocks imitation via automatic exclusive rights

questions.explanation: Faster iteration compresses learning cycles, increasing innovation speed versus rivals.

questions.stem: A firm stalls because rivals iterate faster after initial adoption. Best diagnosis is:

options.A: Patents are too broad, reducing customer adoption
options.B: Radical innovation must never be improved incrementally
options.C: Network effects prevent improvement incentives
options.D: Cadence too slow for accelerating change; learning falls behind

questions.explanation: When change accelerates, slow iteration loses to fast-learning competitors.

questions.stem: A food brand restricts a new recipe process to three executives and never patents it. This is best classified as:

options.A: Chasm strategy because secrecy convinces pragmatists
options.B: Radical innovation because secrecy defines novelty
options.C: Trade secret protection with operational access control
options.D: Platform governance because secrecy solves chicken-or-egg

questions.explanation: Trade secrets are valuable proprietary information kept out of the public domain.

questions.stem: A patent-holder loses advantage because disclosure lets rivals learn quickly. This best reflects:

options.A: The platform chicken-or-egg problem
options.B: The patent disclosure trade-off
options.C: The inevitability of chasm collapse
options.D: The dominance of late-majority adoption

questions.explanation: Disclosure enables learning; rights protect use, but knowledge spreads.

questions.stem: A pharma startup patents a molecule, then incumbents quickly “design around” it. The best interpretation is:

options.A: Patents guarantee adoption because legal rights replace market fit
options.B: Patents eliminate rivalry because substitutes become illegal forever
options.C: Patents grant rights but disclosure can accelerate rival learning
options.D: Patents prevent learning because rivals cannot read patents legally

questions.explanation: Patents can be double-edged: monopoly rights plus disclosure-driven learning.

questions.stem: A press release announces a “revolutionary” concept without a working artifact. The correct label is:

options.A: Innovation because communication equals commercialization
options.B: Imitation because all concepts copy prior work
options.C: Idea, not invention or innovation yet
options.D: Invention because announcing makes it real

questions.explanation: Idea is conceptual; invention needs a working artifact; innovation needs market launch.

questions.stem: A rival copies Netflix’s ad-tier interface but lacks targeting data and experimentation routines. Best inference is:

options.A: Feature imitation always wins because followers avoid early mistakes
options.B: Feature imitation is blocked because ad tiers are patent-protected
options.C: Feature imitation is sufficient because customers see the same tier
options.D: Feature imitation is incomplete without replicating capability systems

questions.explanation: Outcomes depend on underlying learning routines and data assets, not surface features.

questions.stem: A startup says “imitation proves we are losing.” Chapter 7 implies instead:

options.A: Imitation often follows success; the issue becomes renewal
options.B: Imitation is impossible in software markets
options.C: Imitation occurs only after failure, not success
options.D: Imitation occurs only in maturity, not early stages

questions.explanation: Copying can signal success; strategic focus shifts to sustaining advantage.

questions.stem: A startup says “we innovated” because we filed a patent, yet have zero customers. The sharp correction is:

options.A: Innovation requires commercialization and adoption, not filings
options.B: Innovation is identical to invention, so filing is enough
options.C: Patents are innovation because courts validate market demand
options.D: Innovation equals imitation because followers define standards

questions.explanation: Innovation is commercialization; patents alone do not create adoption.

questions.stem: A startup’s edge is a short-lived ranking algorithm in a fast-cycle market. Best appropriability stance is:

options.A: Wait for maturity because early markets punish secrecy
options.B: Broad patents because disclosure prevents competitor learning
options.C: Secrecy and process embedding when enforcement lags market tempo
options.D: No protection because appropriability never matters in tech

questions.explanation: When markets move faster than legal enforcement, secrecy and execution can dominate.

questions.stem: A successful feature is copied within weeks. The most Chapter 7–consistent inference is:

options.A: Imitation follows success; sustain advantage via continuous innovation
options.B: Copying is illegal by default in digital markets
options.C: Copying proves failure; exit because advantage is impossible
options.D: Copying implies radical innovation and permanent monopoly

questions.explanation: In the Four I’s, imitation follows innovation; advantage depends on renewal and complements.

questions.stem: Netflix keeps its recommendation logic unpatented and tightly confidential. This choice best illustrates:

options.A: Patents maximize secrecy and prevent rivals from reading disclosures
options.B: Trade secrets avoid disclosure and preserve algorithmic know-how advantage
options.C: Ideas become innovations once they are published in academic venues
options.D: Imitation reduces risk because followers gain legitimacy through copying

questions.explanation: Patents require disclosure; trade secrets preserve secrecy when disclosure would erase advantage.

questions.stem: Patent expiry followed by entry fits which story best?

options.A: Platform rents replacing patent rents automatically
options.B: Temporary monopoly until imitation/entry accelerates
options.C: Consumer surplus replacing producer capture by definition
options.D: Permanent monopoly because patents never end

questions.explanation: Patents are time-limited; expiry enables easier entry and imitation.

questions.stem: The Four I’s sequence is best captured as:

options.A: Innovation → Imitation → Invention → Idea
options.B: Idea → Innovation → Invention → Imitation
options.C: Idea → Invention → Innovation → Imitation
options.D: Invention → Idea → Imitation → Innovation

questions.explanation: Chapter 7 defines innovation as commercialization after invention, with imitation following success.

questions.stem: The most discriminating test between “invention” and “innovation” is whether:

options.A: Scientists agree it is publishable
options.B: It has a patent number assigned
options.C: Customers adopt it through commercialization at scale
options.D: It uses new technology internally

questions.explanation: Commercialization and adoption are the defining boundary between invention and innovation.

questions.stem: “AI automation may displace routine jobs and shift education returns.” This is tied most to:

options.A: First industrial revolution implications
options.B: Fourth industrial revolution implications
options.C: Third industrial revolution implications
options.D: Second industrial revolution implications

questions.explanation: The fourth industrial revolution emphasizes AI/automation/cyber-physical systems and social impacts.

questions.stem: “Innovation equals invention.” The cleanest rebuttal is:

options.A: Invention is decline; innovation is maturity efficiency
options.B: Invention is imitation; innovation is branding redesign
options.C: Invention is commercialization; innovation is abstract ideation
options.D: Invention is creation; innovation is commercialization and adoption

questions.explanation: Chapter 7 separates invention (artifact) from innovation (commercialization).

questions.stem: A SaaS startup wants to cross the chasm in one vertical before expanding broadly. This is aligned with:

options.A: Decline-stage strategy because chasm crossing is easiest once an industry begins shrinking structurally
options.B: Horizontal strategy to enter all verticals first so early majority can pick any configuration needed
options.C: Laggard-first strategy because laggards are the biggest market and adopt reliably without support
options.D: Beachhead strategy to win one niche with references and whole-product completeness, then expand adjacently

questions.explanation: Chasm crossing favors a focused beachhead to build references and whole product.

questions.stem: A chasm-crossing “beachhead” is mainly used to:

options.A: Target laggards for predictable first adoption
options.B: Create credible references and reduce risk for pragmatists
options.C: Avoid learning and delay commercialization
options.D: Eliminate substitutes through patents

questions.explanation: Beachheads create references and whole-product completeness to reduce pragmatist risk.

questions.stem: A company markets heavily to late majority before fixing early majority concerns. Most likely result:

options.A: Strong adoption, because late majority buys without references, standards, or support
options.B: Weak adoption only if patents exist, because patents make late-majority buyers suspicious
options.C: Weak adoption, because late majority waits for entrenched standards and strong brands built via early majority momentum
options.D: Strong adoption, because late majority values beta testing and tolerates imperfections most

questions.explanation: Late majority generally follows early majority adoption and wants established standards and brands.

questions.stem: A fintech category sees rapid adoption, strong new user growth, and many entrants adding capacity. Stage inference is:

options.A: Decline stage, where demand falls structurally and new entrants avoid the market entirely
options.B: Maturity stage, where replacement dominates and firms compete mainly on incremental efficiency
options.C: Growth stage, where adoption accelerates and entry intensifies as firms pursue scale and position
options.D: Shakeout stage, where exits dominate because consolidation has already reduced competitors

questions.explanation: Growth is rapid adoption plus entry; shakeout is consolidation and exits.

questions.stem: A firm in growth should typically prioritize:

options.A: Harvesting cash immediately
options.B: Eliminating variety to enforce standards
options.C: Scaling while learning and positioning before consolidation arrives
options.D: Exiting early to avoid rivalry

questions.explanation: Growth rewards scaling and positioning; harvest strategies fit later stages.

questions.stem: A firm in introduction stage should typically prioritize:

options.A: Learning fast and finding product–market fit under uncertainty
options.B: Locking standards through scale manufacturing
options.C: Harvesting stable cash flows
options.D: Consolidating competitors

questions.explanation: Introduction is uncertain; learning and early adoption dominate.

questions.stem: A firm tries to cross the chasm by adding features while reliability and support remain weak. The most likely outcome is:

options.A: It succeeds because pragmatists adopt first and prefer novelty even when service is unreliable
options.B: It fails only if patents expire because chasm crossing is mainly a legal exclusivity problem
options.C: It succeeds because features substitute fully for standards, references, and after-sales support
options.D: It still fails because early majority values risk reduction and whole-product support over feature novelty

questions.explanation: Pragmatists value risk reduction and whole-product completeness.

questions.stem: A market shows dominant design, intense rivalry, and exits. Best stage label:

options.A: Growth
options.B: Decline
options.C: Introduction
options.D: Shakeout

questions.explanation: Shakeout features consolidation and exits around a dominant design.

questions.stem: A market shows intense consolidation, exits, and a few surviving leaders around a dominant design. Stage inference is:

options.A: Shakeout stage, where rivalry rises and weaker firms exit as the industry consolidates
options.B: Decline stage, where demand is near zero and firms cannot profitably sell any units
options.C: Introduction stage, where uncertainty falls and designs become more diverse with stable entry
options.D: Growth stage, where entry is high and exits are low because demand is exploding everywhere

questions.explanation: Shakeout is defined by consolidation: rivalry, exits, fewer survivors.

questions.stem: A market shows saturation, slower growth, and competition shifting to incremental improvements and efficiency. Stage inference is:

options.A: Maturity stage, where growth slows and firms compete through efficiency and incremental innovation
options.B: Growth stage, where adoption accelerates and variety expands faster than efficiency pressures
options.C: Shakeout stage, where exits dominate and only a few firms remain after consolidation
options.D: Introduction stage, where uncertainty is highest and designs compete before standards emerge

questions.explanation: Maturity: slower growth, saturation, incremental improvement, efficiency focus.

questions.stem: A micro-mobility industry saw rapid entry and then many exits in several cities. This pattern most closely signals:

options.A: Decline stage completion, where demand collapses to near zero and no replacement cycles remain
options.B: Shakeout stage dynamics, where rivalry intensifies, weaker firms exit, and consolidation accelerates
options.C: Introduction stage stability, where uncertainty drops and competitors converge without exits
options.D: Maturity stage expansion, where entrants proliferate and product variety grows without consolidation

questions.explanation: Shakeout is the consolidation phase after growth, with rising rivalry and exits.

questions.stem: A new consumer device market shows explosive demand growth and many entrants, but standards begin to stabilize. This best fits:

options.A: Shakeout stage, where exits dominate because growth has ended and consolidation is underway
options.B: Decline stage, where demand falls structurally and firms should harvest rather than invest
options.C: Growth stage, where adoption accelerates and entry intensifies while standards start to clarify
options.D: Maturity stage, where replacement dominates and innovation becomes mostly incremental efficiency

questions.explanation: Growth features rapid adoption and entry; standards begin stabilizing.

questions.stem: A product is adopted only when necessary and buyers avoid new technology for personal or economic reasons. This describes:

options.A: Technology enthusiasts, who wait for entrenched standards and strong brands before buying
options.B: Laggards, who enter late and adopt only when adoption becomes unavoidable in practice
options.C: Early adopters, who pay premiums for beta products to signal status and experiment
options.D: Early majority, who adopt early and tolerate uncertainty because novelty is intrinsically valued

questions.explanation: Laggards adopt last and reluctantly; they are rarely the main growth engine.

questions.stem: A smartphone market is replacement-driven with slower growth and intense price competition. The best stage label is:

options.A: Decline stage, where adoption becomes unnecessary and firms should exit immediately and harvest cash
options.B: Maturity stage, where replacement demand rises and rivalry focuses on efficiency and pricing
options.C: Introduction stage, where uncertainty is highest and standards have not emerged across producers
options.D: Growth stage, where first-time adoption dominates and differentiation expands variety without pressure

questions.explanation: Maturity features replacement demand, slower growth, and stronger price rivalry.

questions.stem: A wearable category is still searching for a dominant design and has uncertain standards. The most consistent life-cycle stage is:

options.A: Maturity stage, where standards are entrenched and incremental efficiency becomes the main driver
options.B: Decline stage, where the market contracts and firms harvest rather than invest in new designs
options.C: Introduction stage, where uncertainty is high and designs compete before a dominant design emerges
options.D: Shakeout stage, where dominant design is fully settled and entry accelerates without exits

questions.explanation: Introduction features high uncertainty and competing designs; dominant design tends to emerge later.

questions.stem: A “whole product” emphasis means:

options.A: Price cuts alone with no service investment
options.B: Core product alone with maximum features
options.C: Patent portfolio plus PR campaigns
options.D: Core product plus complements, support, reliability, and standards

questions.explanation: Whole product includes ecosystem elements needed to reduce adoption risk for pragmatists.

questions.stem: An EV startup wins early adopters but loses early majority because repairs take months and service is inconsistent. The best diagnosis is:

options.A: It failed the novelty test, where pragmatists demand unproven experimental features more than reliability
options.B: It failed the ‘whole product’ test, where pragmatists need dependable after-sales support and reliability
options.C: It failed the patent test, where pragmatists refuse products lacking legal exclusivity protections
options.D: It failed the price test, where pragmatists adopt only when prices rise and signal premium quality

questions.explanation: Early majority adoption requires risk reduction: support, standards, and reliability.

questions.stem: Apple Vision Pro’s early buyers were largely enthusiasts and early adopters. In chasm terms, the next major hurdle is convincing the:

options.A: Laggards, who pay premium prices for beta products and tolerate high uncertainty in use
options.B: Technology enthusiasts, who adopt after standards are entrenched and brands are well established
options.C: Early majority, who demand reliability, clear use cases, standards, and strong support before adoption
options.D: Late majority, who purchase first and then create reference cases for other segments to follow

questions.explanation: The key chasm is early adopters → early majority; pragmatists demand whole-product completeness and risk reduction.

questions.stem: Generative AI copilots spread rapidly across teams, then adoption slows as firms demand governance and safety. This slowdown most resembles movement toward:

options.A: Decline stage, where market contraction is dominant and new adoption is structurally impossible
options.B: Technology enthusiast dominance, where beta instability is rewarded because experimentation is the main objective
options.C: Laggard entry, where adoption happens only in decline stage and therefore requires forced compliance
options.D: Early majority concerns, where standards, integration, and risk controls become prerequisites for broad adoption

questions.explanation: Mainstream diffusion slows until standards, integration, reliability, and support are in place.

questions.stem: In decline, the most coherent general move is often:

options.A: Build capacity aggressively for scale
options.B: Harvest or niche-focus rather than broad expansion
options.C: Ignore cash flows and reinvest heavily
options.D: Maximize variety and experimentation

questions.explanation: Decline often calls for harvest/consolidation/niche focus, not broad growth investment.

questions.stem: In maturity, competitive advantage often shifts toward:

options.A: Ignoring customer support and complements
options.B: Incremental innovation and efficiency improvements
options.C: Pure monopoly pricing without value improvements
options.D: Radical category creation only

questions.explanation: Maturity competition often centers on incremental improvements and efficiency.

questions.stem: Late majority is similar to early majority but more risk-averse. The most correct statement is:

options.A: Late majority is similar to early majority but more risk-averse and more brand-dependent in adoption
options.B: Late majority is less risk-averse than early adopters and therefore buys unfinished beta designs first
options.C: Late majority is identical to laggards, so both segments should be pursued aggressively for growth
options.D: Late majority buys mainly for novelty, making standards and support far less important than features

questions.explanation: Late majority prefers established standards and brands, and needs strong support.

questions.stem: Smartphones are in growth in many emerging economies and in maturity in developed economies. The clearest implication is:

options.A: The industry life cycle is invalid because a product cannot be in two stages at the same time
options.B: The shakeout stage is irrelevant because digital goods do not experience consolidation dynamics
options.C: The same firm may need different strategies across geographies because life-cycle stage differs by market
options.D: The decline stage must be next everywhere because maturity in one market forces global contraction

questions.explanation: Life-cycle stages can differ by geography; strategy should adapt accordingly.

questions.stem: Tesla’s Model 3/Model Y are discussed as helping it cross the big chasm. The strategic logic is most directly:

options.A: New patents prevent imitation, pushing adoption from laggards toward early enthusiasts immediately
options.B: Higher-priced models create exclusivity, pushing adoption from late majority toward early adopters
options.C: Network effects guarantee adoption, pushing adoption from early majority toward early adopters over time
options.D: Lower-priced models broaden adoption from early adopters toward the early majority segment

questions.explanation: Lower-priced models expand reachable segments and support mainstream diffusion.

questions.stem: The largest “chasm” is typically between:

options.A: Early majority and laggards
options.B: Technology enthusiasts and laggards
options.C: Late majority and laggards
options.D: Early adopters and early majority

questions.explanation: The major chasm is early adopters → early majority (visionaries → pragmatists).

questions.stem: A cheaper, initially inferior product starts in a fringe segment and later improves to threaten incumbents. The closest label is:

options.A: Disruptive innovation, entering from fringe markets and moving upmarket over time to challenge leaders
options.B: Architectural innovation, applying new technology in existing markets without changing market trajectories
options.C: Incremental innovation, improving existing offerings but never threatening incumbent business models
options.D: Radical innovation, beginning as premium performance and targeting mainstream customers from day one

questions.explanation: Disruptive innovations often begin in fringe/new markets and later move upmarket.

questions.stem: A company builds a new chip architecture but sells it to existing data-center customers. Exhibit 7.12 implies:

options.A: Disruptive innovation, because new chips must start low-end and then move up to mainstream buyers
options.B: Architectural innovation, applying a new technology configuration to an existing market space
options.C: Incremental innovation, because semiconductors only improve steadily without discontinuity by definition
options.D: Radical innovation, because any new technology implies a new market regardless of customer base

questions.explanation: New tech applied to existing markets is architectural innovation.

questions.stem: A firm recombines existing modules for a better experience without new science in the same market. Best label is:

options.A: Disruptive innovation
options.B: Radical innovation
options.C: Architectural innovation
options.D: Incremental innovation

questions.explanation: Same market + same tech base recombination typically remains incremental.

questions.stem: A firm reconfigures existing components into a new system architecture for its current customer base without new science. The closest label is:

options.A: Architectural innovation, because any internal redesign necessarily creates a new market by definition
options.B: Disruptive innovation, because system redesigns always begin low-end and then displace premium incumbents
options.C: Radical innovation, because recombination always implies a new market and a new technology knowledge base
options.D: Incremental innovation, because it recombines existing knowledge for existing markets without new technology bases

questions.explanation: Recombination within existing markets/tech base is typically incremental.

questions.stem: A firm sells a premium product that improves mainstream performance and calls it disruptive. Best critique is:

options.A: Definitely disruptive because premium implies new market
options.B: Likely sustaining improvement, not classic disruption trajectory
options.C: Not classifiable because disruption depends only on patents
options.D: Definitely disruptive because better performance defines disruption

questions.explanation: Premium sustaining improvements are not the classic disruptive trajectory.

questions.stem: A firm uses existing tech to reach customers previously outside the category. That is most consistent with:

options.A: Architectural innovation
options.B: Incremental innovation
options.C: Disruptive innovation
options.D: Radical innovation

questions.explanation: New market served with existing technology aligns with architectural innovation.

questions.stem: A firm uses new tech to sell to existing customers. That is most consistent with:

options.A: Architectural innovation
options.B: Disruptive innovation
options.C: Incremental innovation
options.D: Radical innovation

questions.explanation: New technology applied to an existing market is architectural innovation.

questions.stem: A firm’s radical breakthrough is followed by many small upgrades. The best interpretation is:

options.A: Radical creates lead; incremental sustains advantage over time
options.B: Radical makes incremental illegal
options.C: Disruption requires only one upgrade cycle
options.D: Incremental makes radical impossible

questions.explanation: Common pattern: radical innovation creates a lead; incremental sustains it.

questions.stem: A new gene-editing therapy creates a new category and new market applications. In Exhibit 7.12, it best fits:

options.A: Disruptive innovation, starting low-end in existing markets and then improving to match incumbents
options.B: Architectural innovation, targeting new markets using existing technologies without new science
options.C: Incremental innovation, improving existing offerings for existing markets using existing technologies
options.D: Radical innovation, targeting new markets by using new technologies from novel knowledge bases

questions.explanation: Radical innovation is new tech plus new market, often creating new industries.

questions.stem: A premium, higher-performance product is called “disruptive.” The best critique is:

options.A: That pattern resembles sustaining improvement; disruption typically enters fringe or new markets first
options.B: That pattern is disruptive by definition, because disruption equals superior performance at launch
options.C: That pattern is architectural by definition, because premium products always target existing markets
options.D: That pattern is radical by definition, because premium implies new market creation automatically

questions.explanation: Disruption is a trajectory and entry pattern, not simply “better and pricier.”

questions.stem: A product based on new materials and methods targets a new application market. Exhibit 7.12 label is:

options.A: Architectural innovation, using existing technologies to create a new market without new knowledge
options.B: Radical innovation, combining new technologies with new markets and sometimes creating new industries
options.C: Incremental innovation, improving existing products for existing markets with existing technologies
options.D: Disruptive innovation, entering existing markets at premium tiers and then moving downmarket

questions.explanation: New tech + new market is radical innovation.

questions.stem: A smartphone maker upgrades camera software and battery management using the same chip platform for current users. Exhibit 7.12 label is:

options.A: Disruptive innovation, starting low-end and then moving upmarket as incumbents overshoot demand
options.B: Incremental innovation, improving existing products in existing markets using existing technologies
options.C: Architectural innovation, creating new markets using existing technologies without altering the product
options.D: Radical innovation, creating new markets because any improvement creates a new category of buyers

questions.explanation: Existing tech + existing market improvements are incremental.

questions.stem: A startup uses existing payment rails but targets newly served segments in a new market. Exhibit 7.12 suggests:

options.A: Disruptive innovation, requiring inferior quality and low price as a necessary condition always
options.B: Radical innovation, requiring new technologies whenever a new segment is targeted at all
options.C: Architectural innovation, using existing technologies to create or serve a new market space
options.D: Incremental innovation, improving existing offerings for existing markets using the same technology

questions.explanation: New market + existing tech aligns with architectural innovation in Exhibit 7.12.

questions.stem: Amazon improves Alexa with better speech recognition using existing ML methods for existing customers. In Exhibit 7.12 terms, this is:

options.A: Incremental innovation, improving an existing offering for existing markets using existing technologies
options.B: Disruptive innovation, entering a new fringe market and later moving upmarket to displace incumbents
options.C: Architectural innovation, creating a new market using existing technologies with no change in use
options.D: Radical innovation, creating a new market using new technologies that replace prior knowledge bases

questions.explanation: Incremental innovation improves existing offerings for existing markets using existing technologies.

questions.stem: An IoT cyber-physical system linking devices and analytics is most associated with:

options.A: The fourth industrial revolution with AI, automation, robotics, and IoT cyber-physical systems
options.B: The second industrial revolution driven by electrification and mass production
options.C: The first industrial revolution driven by steam power and mechanization
options.D: The third industrial revolution driven by computers but not connected cyber-physical systems

questions.explanation: Chapter 7 associates IoT and cyber-physical systems with the fourth industrial revolution.

questions.stem: Disruptive innovation is best described as:

options.A: Entry via fringe/new markets with different attributes, then upmarket movement
options.B: New technology plus new market always
options.C: Immediate domination of mainstream markets through superior premium performance
options.D: Existing technology plus existing market always

questions.explanation: Disruption is about entry footholds and trajectory, not immediate premium superiority.

questions.stem: Existing tech + existing market improvements generally classify as:

options.A: Architectural
options.B: Incremental
options.C: Disruptive
options.D: Radical

questions.explanation: That is the incremental quadrant in the markets–technology framework.

questions.stem: Existing tech + new market generally classify as:

options.A: Incremental
options.B: Radical
options.C: Architectural
options.D: Disruptive

questions.explanation: Existing technologies serving a new market is architectural innovation.

questions.stem: Fourth industrial revolution dynamics are most likely to increase returns to:

options.A: Education and adaptable human capital, because routine tasks are more automatable
options.B: Corporate secrecy, because diffusion becomes impossible once automation expands
options.C: Inventory stockpiles, because scarcity becomes the main source of advantage
options.D: Retail floor space, because foot traffic is the central moat in cyber-physical markets

questions.explanation: As automation rises, the value of adaptable skills and education increases.

questions.stem: New tech + existing market generally classify as:

options.A: Disruptive
options.B: Radical
options.C: Incremental
options.D: Architectural

questions.explanation: New tech applied to an existing market is architectural innovation.

questions.stem: New tech + new market creation generally classify as:

options.A: Radical
options.B: Architectural
options.C: Incremental
options.D: Disruptive

questions.explanation: New technologies aimed at new markets map to radical innovation.

questions.stem: The diagonal pairing in the framework highlights:

options.A: Incremental vs radical, and architectural vs disruptive
options.B: Incremental vs architectural only
options.C: Disruptive vs incremental only
options.D: Radical vs disruptive only

questions.explanation: Two diagonal contrasts: incremental–radical and architectural–disruptive.

questions.stem: The most diagnostic question for classification is:

options.A: Profit margin changes in the first quarter
options.B: Legal disputes and patent filings
options.C: Influencer engagement and brand mentions
options.D: Existing vs new markets, and existing vs new technologies

questions.explanation: The framework is defined by market newness and technology newness.

questions.stem: “Most innovations are radical.” The best correction is:

options.A: Most innovations are incremental, despite attention to breakthroughs
options.B: Most innovations are architectural only
options.C: Most innovations are disruptive, not incremental
options.D: Most innovations are radical because markets demand novelty

questions.explanation: Chapter 7 stresses that incremental innovations dominate in practice.

questions.stem: “New to our firm” does not necessarily mean “radical.” The correct diagnostic is:

options.A: Newness to market and technology axes, not internal novelty
options.B: Patent status and court enforceability
options.C: Marketing excitement and press coverage intensity
options.D: Founder charisma and early funding size

questions.explanation: Classification depends on market newness and technology newness, not internal unfamiliarity.

questions.stem: A creator platform solves chicken-or-egg by guaranteeing buyers for first creators. This is:

options.A: Decline-stage repositioning
options.B: Architectural innovation classification
options.C: Harvesting demand in maturity stage
options.D: Seeding one side to create early proof and transactions

questions.explanation: Seeding generates liquidity and proof that attracts the other side.

questions.stem: A platform adds complements through third parties. Most accurate implication is:

options.A: Less value potential because complements always cannibalize
options.B: Governance becomes unnecessary because complements self-police
options.C: Network effects become irrelevant once complements exist
options.D: More value potential, but governance complexity rises sharply

questions.explanation: Complements expand value but increase rule-setting and enforcement needs.

questions.stem: A platform becomes valuable because more users join, not because unit costs fall. This is:

options.A: Economies of scale, not network effects
options.B: Life-cycle maturity, not platform dynamics
options.C: Network effects, not just economies of scale
options.D: Radical innovation, not platform dynamics

questions.explanation: Network effects are demand-side; scale economies are supply-side.

questions.stem: A platform competitor copies the interface but lacks users. Why does it matter?

options.A: Inventory ownership is the key; users are secondary
options.B: Advertising alone creates value; user counts are irrelevant
options.C: Without critical mass, network effects are weak and value is lower
options.D: Interface copying is illegal so users automatically migrate

questions.explanation: The network is the product; without participation on both sides, value collapses.

questions.stem: A platform lowers take rate to attract more producers, expecting later growth. This is:

options.A: Crossing the chasm by targeting laggards first
options.B: Eliminating substitutes by predatory pricing
options.C: Converting invention into innovation automatically
options.D: Subsidizing one side to ignite participation and network effects

questions.explanation: Subsidies can build critical mass and ignite network effects.

questions.stem: A platform opens APIs for complements but fails to enforce quality rules. Primary risk is:

options.A: Trust collapses; participation falls; network effects weaken
options.B: Patents prevent low-quality participants from joining
options.C: Trust increases automatically through openness
options.D: Complements matter only in late majority stage

questions.explanation: Openness without governance invites adverse selection and erodes trust.

questions.stem: A platform raises take rates aggressively before stabilizing network effects. Risk is:

options.A: Substitutes vanish because users lock in
options.B: Chasm becomes irrelevant because fees imply reliability
options.C: Rivals exit because fees signal quality
options.D: Participation drops and network effects weaken

questions.explanation: Premature monetization can reduce participation before critical mass, weakening network effects.

questions.stem: A platform restricts third-party producers “to stay in control.” Core risk is:

options.A: Chicken-or-egg disappears because restriction forces joining
options.B: Network effects strengthen because fewer producers increases value
options.C: Ecosystem growth slows; network effects fail to scale
options.D: Chasm crossing becomes automatic because closure signals reliability

questions.explanation: Restriction can throttle variety and participation, weakening network effects.

questions.stem: A platform stagnates after trust scandals. Best explanation is:

options.A: Trust scandals push adoption to late majority faster
options.B: Trust scandals prove radical innovation is occurring
options.C: Reduced participation weakens network effects and value for remaining users
options.D: Trust scandals reduce costs and improve margins

questions.explanation: Participation shocks can trigger negative spirals in network-effect markets.

questions.stem: A platform’s feedback loops create advantage mainly by:

options.A: Eliminating the need for governance and moderation
options.B: Making patents unnecessary for all industries
options.C: Replacing the need for supply-side growth
options.D: Improving match quality and reducing friction through data learning

questions.explanation: Platforms learn from interactions; better matching improves value creation.

questions.stem: A platform’s governance is best seen as:

options.A: A substitute for product design and customer experience
options.B: A late-stage activity only after maturity arrives
options.C: A compliance detail unrelated to platform economics
options.D: A strategic lever shaping value creation and participation quality

questions.explanation: Governance shapes trust and participation—core to platform advantage.

questions.stem: A platform’s “product” includes:

options.A: Only the HR hiring system
options.B: Rules, trust mechanisms, incentives, and matching infrastructure
options.C: Only the user interface and brand slogan
options.D: Only the financing structure and capital policy

questions.explanation: Platform strategy is ecosystem design: roles, incentives, governance, and matching.

questions.stem: A rider becomes a driver within the same platform. This is:

options.A: Architectural innovation
options.B: Multi-homing
options.C: Side switching
options.D: Chasm crossing

questions.explanation: Side switching is movement across roles within the same platform ecosystem.

questions.stem: A social enterprise earns revenue and also measures social outcomes. That fits best with:

options.A: Social entrepreneurship definition used in this chapter
options.B: Decline-stage harvest strategy
options.C: Strategic entrepreneurship only
options.D: Pure imitation strategy

questions.explanation: Social entrepreneurship integrates mission with viable venture logic.

questions.stem: Airbnb scales supply without owning hotels mainly because it:

options.A: Vertically integrates real estate to lower costs
options.B: Unlocks external supply through hosts in an asset-light manner
options.C: Eliminates the need for governance because trust is automatic
options.D: Crosses the chasm by targeting laggards first

questions.explanation: Platforms scale by enrolling ecosystem participants rather than owning assets.

questions.stem: Chicken-or-egg problem at launch is best solved by:

options.A: Removing all rules to maximize entry
options.B: Waiting until both sides are naturally large
options.C: Seeding/subsidizing one side to create early transactions
options.D: Raising fees early to signal quality

questions.explanation: Platforms seed one side to create proof that attracts the other side.

questions.stem: Fraud/spam drives users away on a marketplace. The key platform lesson is:

options.A: Governance matters only for pipelines with inventory
options.B: Governance always hurts adoption; remove rules immediately
options.C: Governance is irrelevant; network effects are mechanical
options.D: Governance sustains trust; weak rules can collapse network effects

questions.explanation: Platforms must govern participation quality; trust failures reduce participation and value.

questions.stem: More merchants accept a card network → more consumers carry it → more merchants join. This is:

options.A: Decline-stage replacement demand
options.B: Cross-side network effects
options.C: Economies of scale only
options.D: Radical innovation automatically

questions.explanation: Two-sided platforms benefit when each side’s participation increases value for the other.

questions.stem: Multi-homing best describes:

options.A: A participant using multiple platforms at the same time
options.B: A participant switching from consumer to producer
options.C: A firm shifting from incremental to radical innovation
options.D: A firm moving from introduction to maturity stage

questions.explanation: Multi-homing is simultaneous participation across platforms.

questions.stem: Platform vs pipeline is best distinguished by whether the firm:

options.A: Orchestrates interactions among external parties or owns production linearly
options.B: Operates globally or locally
options.C: Uses technology or not
options.D: Is venture-funded or not

questions.explanation: Core distinction: matching/orchestration vs linear production/ownership.

questions.stem: Social entrepreneurship (as used here) is best described as:

options.A: Pursuing social goals via ventures using triple-bottom-line performance
options.B: Platform-only strategy because networks create all social value
options.C: Maximizing profit only and treating impact as externality
options.D: Radical-only innovation because incremental cannot help society

questions.explanation: Social entrepreneurship integrates mission with venture logic and triple-bottom-line metrics.

questions.stem: Strategic entrepreneurship is best described as:

options.A: Copying incumbents only to reduce novelty risk
options.B: Using strategy tools to build ventures that create and capture value
options.C: Harvesting declining markets as a startup default
options.D: Doing philanthropy first and revenue later

questions.explanation: Strategic entrepreneurship applies strategic-management concepts to venture building.

questions.stem: Uber’s ride-hailing model is best classified as:

options.A: Radical: new tech plus new market by definition
options.B: Pipeline: owns production and sells linearly
options.C: Incremental: cannot change industry economics
options.D: Platform: matches external producers and consumers

questions.explanation: Platforms orchestrate interactions between external sides; pipelines own and push outputs.

questions.stem: “Platforms always outperform pipelines.” Best caveat is:

options.A: Only if positive network effects and governance are achieved
options.B: True only with radical technology, not business design
options.C: Always true by definition, regardless of execution
options.D: True only in decline stage, not in growth stage

questions.explanation: Platform outperformance depends on achieving positive network effects with governance.

questions.stem: “We are a platform” but the firm owns inventory, sets prices, and sells directly. Best diagnosis:

options.A: Radical innovation because inventory implies novelty
options.B: Mostly pipeline with digital distribution
options.C: True platform because any app is multi-sided
options.D: Social entrepreneurship because intermediation helps society

questions.explanation: Owning inventory and selling outputs is pipeline logic; platforms match external producers/consumers.
